data.source: National Oesophago-Gastric Cancer Audit 2023 data tables, 2019-22 (CC BY, HQIP).
data.caveat: The audit's own finding: every centre was within the expected range for 90-day mortality (one was outside for 30-day). The spread you see in the raw percentages is within statistical noise — so this is not a league table. In a centralised system the question shifts from 'will I die here' to readmission, length of stay, and whether curative surgery is offered at all.

reading: The table shows each centre’s adjusted 30‑day and 90‑day death rates after oesophagectomy, based on the number of operations they performed between 2019‑22. Most centres report very low 30‑day rates (often 0 % or under 1 %), while 90‑day rates range from about 0.9 % up to 7.4 %. Because the audit found that every centre’s 90‑day mortality lies within the expected range – the differences you see are likely just random variation – these percentages cannot tell you which hospital is safer for you. They also do not show other important factors such as readmission, length of stay, or whether curative surgery is routinely offered. When deciding where to have your operation, consider asking your surgical team about their experience, the support services available, and how they handle complications, rather than relying solely on these mortality figures.

judgment.volume_verdict: Mixed — US data show lower mortality at higher-volume hospitals but surgeon outcomes vary widely even above volume thresholds, while English centralisation eliminated 90-day mortality outliers so volume is not the signal there.
judgment.explanation: Kalata 2024 found 30-day mortality of 8.1% at low-volume US hospitals versus 5.5% at hospitals meeting a volume standard (adjusted OR 0.67), yet Cancer 2021 reported 90-day mortality ranging from 3.5% to 9.3% even among surgeons who met that volume bar. Wasif 2020 showed volume thresholds had only 24–26% positive predictive value for identifying poor-performing hospitals, and the NOGCA 2026 audit confirmed that after centralisation in England no surgical centre was a 90-day mortality outlier — though readmission (7–29%) and long stays (11–40%) still varied.
do_not: Assume that choosing a high-volume hospital guarantees a better outcome for you.
Treat the adjusted mortality percentages in the NOGCA table as a league table — the audit states the spread is within statistical noise.
Conclude that volume alone tells you whether a centre is safe; the English data show mortality outliers disappeared after centralisation, but other quality markers still differ.
judgment.next_step: Ask your surgical team for their centre's 90-day mortality, readmission rate, and median length of stay, and request a second-opinion review if your case is borderline for curative surgery.

questions: How many of these operations have you personally done, and how many in the last year?
How do your own results — mortality, serious complications — compare with other centres?
Is there a hospital nearby that does more of these, and would you refer me there?

evidence.finding: 30-day mortality was 8.1% at low-volume hospitals versus 5.5% at hospitals meeting the volume standard (adjusted odds ratio 0.67). For 79.8% of operations done at a low-volume hospital, a hospital meeting the standard sat in the same insurance network, a median of 29 miles from the patient's home.
Even among surgeons who met the volume standard, 90-day esophagectomy mortality ranged from 3.5% to 9.3%. Meeting a volume bar is not the same as a good outcome.

evidence.cite: Wasif et al., J Am Coll Surg 2020;231(1):45-52
evidence.finding: Leapfrog volume thresholds had a positive predictive value of only 24-26% for identifying poor-performing hospitals. Case-volume cut-offs alone do not track actual hospital mortality well.

evidence.cite: National Oesophago-Gastric Cancer Audit, State of the Nation 2026 (HQIP)
evidence.finding: After England centralised oesophago-gastric cancer surgery, 90-day survival after curative surgery was 96.7% and no surgical centre was a 90-day mortality outlier. But length of stay over 15 days ranged 11%-40% between centres and 30-day readmission ranged 7%-29%; and only 67% of fit stage 1-3 patients started curative treatment. The audit says a second-opinion review 'may be beneficial' in borderline cases.
